documents.content: For the resistor branch, the constitutive relation is $V=IR$.
The branch current follows from \[I=\frac{V}{R}\].
For a measured operating point, use $R=\frac{V}{I}$.
The source resistor obeys \[V_s=I_sR_s\].
Across terminals \(a\) and \(b\), the passive-sign relation is $V_{ab}=R_b I_{ab}$.
For an ideal time-invariant resistor, \[v(t)=R\,i(t)\].
Solving the same device law for current gives $i(t)=v(t)/R$.
The labeled element satisfies \[V_R=R\,I_R\].
Let \(\Delta V\) be the signed drop. Then $\Delta V=I_\ell R_\ell$.
Here \(E\) denotes the voltage across the resistor, \(J\) its current, and \(\rho\) its resistance; $E=J\rho$.
Using \(U\) for voltage, the resistor equation is \[U=R I\].
The lab sheet presents the relation with the product first: \[I R=V\].
For clarity, the report groups the measured factors as $V=(I)(R)$.
The asserted device law is \[(V)=(R\,I)\].
Let \(V_d\) denote voltage drop, \(I_d\) branch current, and \(R_d\) resistance. The model uses $V_d=I_dR_d$.
The branch model is \[e_b=j_b r_b\]. Here \(e_b\), \(j_b\), and \(r_b\) denote voltage, current, and resistance respectively.
With current \(i_L\) directed into the marked terminal, $v_L=R_L i_L$ gives the load voltage.
Voltages are reported in volts, currents in amperes, and resistance in ohms; the symbolic relation is \[V_m=I_mR_m\].
Using the project voltage alias, the component equation is $\Vdrop=I R$.
The schematic notation states \[\Volt=\Ampere\,\Ohmic\].
For the marked positive voltage terminal and entering current arrow, \[v_+=r_p i_+\].
The load line uses $V_{\mathrm{load}}=I_{\mathrm{load}}R_{\mathrm{load}}$.
For sensor branch \(3\), \[v_3=i_3 r_3\].
The inferred element value is $\mathcal{R}_x=V_x/I_x$, where \(\mathcal{R}_x\) is resistance.
The selected row of the derivation is \[\begin{aligned}V_o&=I_oR_o\end{aligned}\].
The final component model is highlighted as \[\boxed{V_c=R_c I_c}\].
After isolating current, the worksheet obtains \[i_x=\left(\frac{v_x}{r_x}\right)\].

Voltage \(V_h\) is measured across the heater.
Current \(I_h\) enters its positive terminal and \(R_h\) is its resistance.
Thus \[V_h=R_h I_h\].

\input{symbols}
The resistor equation is \[V_b=I_bR_b\].
In this project \(V_b\) is voltage, \(I_b\) is current, and \(R_b\) is resistance.

\input{notation}
The branch law is $\BranchV=\BranchI\BranchR$.
The proposed relation is $V=I+R$, which combines unlike roles additively.
The nonlinear expression \[V=IR^2\] is not the ideal resistor law.
The draft claims $V=R/I$ for the branch.
Here \(R\) is declared to be current, \(I\) resistance, and \(V\) voltage, followed by \[V=IR\].
Current enters the positive-voltage terminal, yet the sheet asserts $V=-IR$.
With \(G\) declared as conductance, the valid but different relation is \[I=GV\].
For an AC impedance \(Z\), the phasors satisfy $\tilde V=\tilde I Z$.
The power identity \[P=VI\] is present, but no resistance law is asserted.
The capacitor relation $V=Q/C$ concerns charge and capacitance.
The loop equation \[V_1=V_2+V_3\] relates only voltages.
The device is explicitly nonlinear and follows $V=kI^2$.
Only the small-signal increments obey \[dV=r_d\,dI\]; this does not establish a global static law.
The regression reports merely $V\approx IR$ over the sampled range.
A safety constraint imposes \[V\leq IR\] rather than an equality.
The document declares \(I\) in volts and \(V\) in amperes, then writes $V=IR$.
The manual explicitly says that $V=IR$ does not apply to this diode.
If the unknown element were an ideal resistor, one could test \[V=IR\], but its type is not known.
In the control model, \(I\) names a function and the expression is $V=I(R)$, not a current-times-resistance product.
Without any definition of the alias, the report contains $\mysteryOhm{V}{I}{R}$.
Two incompatible candidates are listed: $V=IR$ for model A and \(V=-IR\) for model B, with no selected model.
At node \(n\), the entering currents balance the leaving branch: $I_1+I_2=I_3$.
The junction equation is \[I_{\mathrm{in}}=I_a+I_b\].
With entering currents positive, the node law is $I_a+I_b-I_c=0$.
The same node balance is displayed as \[0=I_p+I_q-I_r\].
Using outward reference directions, KCL gives $\sum_{k=1}^{m} I_k=0$.
The aggregate statement is \[\sum_{j\in\mathrm{in}}i_j=\sum_{j\in\mathrm{out}}i_j\].
At node \(A\), the labeled branches satisfy $I_{A1}+I_{A2}=I_{A3}$.
Instantaneously, \[i_1(t)+i_2(t)=i_3(t)\] at the junction.
The source current splits according to $I_S=I_L+I_B$.
The report writes the outgoing side first: \[I_o+I_p=I_s\].
For presentation, the balance is $(I_1+I_2)=(I_3+I_4)$.
The selected node equation is \[\boxed{i_a+i_b-i_c-i_d=0}\].
Let \(j_1,j_2\) enter the node and \(j_3\) leave it. Then $j_1+j_2=j_3$.
The junction obeys \[a+b=c\]. Here \(a,b\) are entering currents and \(c\) is the leaving current.
All four branch arrows point away from the node, so $i_a+i_b+i_c+i_d=0$.
With every arrow defined toward the node, the signed currents satisfy \[j_a+j_b+j_c=0\].
The measured negative branch value is retained in $I_1+(-I_2)+I_3=0$.
At the distribution node, \[I_{\rm feed}=I_1+I_2+I_3\].
For the transistor terminal currents, the node equation is $i_e=i_b+i_c$.
At the AC node the phasor currents obey \[\tilde I_1+\tilde I_2=\tilde I_3\].
The derivation isolates the node row as \[\begin{aligned}I_x+I_y-I_z&=0\end{aligned}\].
The flow groups are shown as $\underbrace{I_a+I_b}_{\rm entering}=\underbrace{I_c+I_d}_{\rm leaving}$.
Currents \(p\) and \(q\) enter, while currents \(r\) and \(s\) leave. Conservation gives \[p+q=r+s\].
Every branch quantity is measured in amperes, and the junction balance is $J_0-J_1-J_2=0$.
The equation \[k_1+k_2=k_3\] applies specifically at node \(N_7\); all three symbols denote branch currents.
The two feeders satisfy $I_{\mathrm{in},1}+I_{\mathrm{in},2}=I_{\mathrm{out}}$.
Relative to reference node \(n_0\), \[i_{n0,1}-i_{n0,2}+i_{n0,3}=0\].
The aliased branch currents satisfy $\InOne+\InTwo=\OutOne$.

\input{branches}
At node \(q\), \[I_u+I_v=I_w\].
Symbols \(I_u,I_v\) are entering currents and \(I_w\) is the outgoing current.

\input{node-macros}
The node law is $\Feed=\LoadA+\LoadB$.
The loop equation $\sum_{k=1}^{3}V_k=0$ sums voltages, not node currents.
The expression \[P_1+P_2-P_3=0\] is a power balance.
The stored charges satisfy $Q_1+Q_2=Q_3$, without a current statement.
The measured node has an unexplained residual: \[I_1+I_2-I_3=\epsilon\].
A current limit imposes $I_1+I_2\leq I_{\max}$.
The expression \[I_1I_2=I_3\] multiplies branch currents.
The gain relation $I_o/I_i=\beta$ is not a node conservation equation.
The identity \[i=dq/dt\] defines current from charge flow but does not balance a node.
The isolated equality $I_1=I_2$ gives no node, directions, or conservation scope.
Because charge accumulates in the modeled region, the text says $I_1+I_2=I_3$ must not be imposed.
If the connector were ideal, one might write \[I_a+I_b=I_c\], but leakage is unspecified.
All three arrows are declared entering the node, yet the report uses $I_1+I_2-I_3=0$ without assigning \(I_3\) a negative value.
Here \(I_a\) and \(I_b\) are currents but \(V_c\) is a voltage; \[I_a+I_b=V_c\] is dimensionally invalid.
No definition is provided for the assertion $\mysteryNode{I_1}{I_2}{I_3}$.
The unscoped line $I_1+I_2=I_3+I_4$ combines labels from two different nodes according to the schematic.
The accumulated charge relation is \[\int_0^T I_1\,dt=\int_0^T I_2\,dt\], not an instantaneous node balance.
The symbols are probabilities, and $p_1+p_2+p_3=1$ normalizes outcomes.
The constraint \[(I_1,I_2)\in\mathcal{F}\] only states feasible current pairs.
The quantities are declared as \(I_1=2\,\mathrm{A}\), \(I_2=3\,\mathrm{A}\), and \(I_3=5\,\mathrm{V}\), followed by $I_1+I_2=I_3$.
Two captions assign opposite directions to \(I_b\), so the candidate equation \[I_a+I_b=I_c\] has no unambiguous sign convention.
For the ideal capacitor, the passive-sign relation is $i=C\frac{dv}{dt}$.
The labeled component obeys \[I_C=C\frac{dV_C}{dt}\].
From a transient measurement, compute $C=\frac{i}{dv/dt}$.
The voltage slope is \[\frac{dv}{dt}=\frac{i}{C}\].
With explicit time dependence, $i(t)=C\,\frac{d v(t)}{dt}$.
The same constitutive law in dot notation is \[i(t)=C\dot v(t)\].
For the transient waveform, $I_c=C_c\dot V_c$.
The worksheet writes the derivative product first: \[C\,\frac{dV}{dt}=I\].
The constitutive equation is presented as $(i)=\left(C\,dv/dt\right)$.
Across terminals \(a,b\), \[i_{ab}=C_{ab}\frac{dv_{ab}}{dt}\].
Let \(j\) be capacitor current, \(K\) capacitance, and \(u\) terminal voltage. Then $j=K\,du/dt$.
The device follows \[a=B\dot e\]. Here \(a\) is current, \(B\) capacitance, and \(e\) voltage.
Current \(j_x\) enters the positive terminal, \(u_x\) is its voltage, and \(K_x\) is capacitance; $j_x=K_x\frac{du_x}{dt}$.
Using the project voltage alias, the capacitor law is $i=C\frac{d\CapV}{dt}$.
The aliased transient equation is \[\CapI=\CapC\,\dot{\CapV}\].
The derivation highlights \[\begin{aligned}i_o&=C_o\frac{dv_o}{dt}\end{aligned}\].
The final capacitor model is \[\boxed{I_x=C_x\dot V_x}\].
At the sample instant, \[i(\tau)=C\left.\frac{dv}{dt}\right|_{t=\tau}\].
Using \(u\) for voltage, the element law is $i_c=C_c\,du_c/dt$.
The current symbol \(j(t)\) is defined by \[j(t)=C_s\dot v_s(t)\].
For capacitance \(K_m\), the law reads $i_m=K_m\,v_m'$.
The storage element satisfies \[I_{\mathrm{cap}}=C_{\mathrm{cap}}\frac{dV_{\mathrm{cap}}}{dt}\].
Current \(i_{\rm out}\) is referenced leaving the positive-voltage terminal, so \[i_{\rm out}=-C\,dv/dt\].
With \(D_t\) denoting time differentiation, the model is $i=C D_t v$.
The prime denotes differentiation with respect to time in \[i_q=C_q v_q'\].
With capacitance in farads and voltage slope in volts per second, $I_m=C_m\,dV_m/dt$ yields amperes.
The notation deliberately spaces the differential: \[i_z=C_z\,\frac{\mathrm d v_z}{\mathrm d t}\].
The current relation is $i_n=C_n\left(\frac{dv_n}{dt}\right)$.

\input{cap-symbols}
The element obeys \[j_f=K_f\frac{du_f}{dt}\].
Here \(j_f\) is current, \(K_f\) capacitance, and \(u_f\) voltage.

\input{cap-notation}
The transient law is $\StoreI=\StoreC\dot{\StoreV}$.
The equation $i=V/R$ is a resistor current law, not a capacitor derivative law.
The display \[v=L\frac{di}{dt}\] describes an inductor.
The draft incorrectly writes $i=C\frac{di}{dt}$, differentiating current instead of voltage.
The expression \[i=C+\frac{dv}{dt}\] adds capacitance to a voltage slope.
The proposed model $i=\frac{1}{C}\frac{dv}{dt}$ uses reciprocal capacitance.
The static expression \[i=Cv\] omits time differentiation.
The nonlinear candidate is $i=C(dv/dt)^2$.
Current is declared entering the positive terminal, but the formula is \[i=-C\,dv/dt\].
Current is declared leaving the positive terminal, yet the document asserts $i=C\,dv/dt$.
The symbol \(C\) is declared to be resistance in ohms, followed by \[i=C\,dv/dt\].
For the nonlinear dielectric, the text explicitly says $i=C\,dv/dt$ is not valid.
If the device capacitance were constant, one could use \[i=C\,dv/dt\], but \(C\) is stated to vary.
No macro definition accompanies $\mysteryCap{i}{C}{v}{t}$.
Here \(C\) is explicitly the speed of light, so $i=C\,dv/dt$ cannot be a capacitance law.
The field profile uses \[i=C\frac{dv}{dx}\], a spatial derivative rather than a time derivative.
The numerical approximation $i\approx C\frac{v_{n+1}-v_n}{\Delta t}$ is not asserted as an exact constitutive equation.
The candidate \[i=C\int_0^t v(\tau)\,d\tau\] integrates voltage instead of differentiating it.
The related identity $q=CV$ states charge versus voltage but not capacitor current.
The capacitance is \(C(t)\), yet the document drops the product derivative and claims \[i=C(t)\frac{dv}{dt}\] without assuming \(\dot C=0\).
Two diagrams assign opposite current arrows, so the isolated candidate $i=C\,dv/dt$ has no resolvable sign convention.
